Read-only research, "very thorough". Windows machine. I am writing Eric's ideal daily workflow guide (morning login → night logout) and need an accurate picture of the AUTOMATION layer around his Claude Code skills. Do not read the skills' SKILL.md files in depth (another agent covers skills).

Find and summarize:
1. Memory notes on cadence/routines. Read these files fully (Tier A memory dir C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\projects\C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV\memory\): project_automation-cadence.md, feedback_session-hygiene.md, project_supervisor-log-pipeline.md, project_status-report-sourcing.md, project_prioritization-slate.md, project_command-centre.md, project_backup-sync-system.md, project_memory-compiler-pipeline.md, project_cfb-forecast-capture.md, project_morning-briefing-retired.md, user_working-conditions-bottleneck.md, project_keystoneos-verification-habits.md. Also C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\global-memory\USER.md and MEMORY.md.
2. Claude Code mods: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\mods\README.md and each mod's slash commands (/pm, /landed, /slate, /repos, /jobs, /where, /twins, /encoding, /next-steps …) — one line each: what it shows, when it fires.
3. Hooks: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\settings.json "hooks" section — list each event (SessionStart, Stop, PreCompact, UserPromptSubmit…) and what script runs and what it does (one line each; peek at the scripts in ~/.claude/hooks or ~/.claude/scripts only enough to say what they do).
4. Scheduled jobs on THIS machine: run `schtasks /query /fo csv /v` and list tasks related to Eric's setup (KeystoneOS, backup, memory compiler, flush, memsearch, harvest, etc.): name, schedule, enabled/disabled, last run, what it runs. Also note what the memory notes say runs on the Mac (launchd).
5. Scripts Eric runs by hand: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\scripts\ (where-was-i.py, session-sweep.py, dev-activity, harvest-dev-docs …) one line each.
6. KeystoneOS rituals: C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\KeystoneOS\scripts\ritual-check.ps1 and its docs/STATUS.md — what rituals exist and their expected cadence.
7. C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\COMMANDS.md — summarize its sections (section titles + the commands that matter for a daily routine).
8. Any doc that already describes a daily/weekly routine or "operating cadence" (e.g. SecondBrain/Projects/Applied-Performance-Operating-Cadence.md under C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain, KeystoneOS AGENTS.md/docs). Summarize what it prescribes.
9. Machine split facts: which work is Windows-day vs Mac-evening, Mac-only jobs (GPS/Perch/VALD, CFB capture).

Return a structured digest with file paths for every claim. Mark anything stale/retired as such (e.g. morning-briefing retired, command centre launchd being retired, KeystoneOS Morning task disabled). Don't guess.
<context_window_protection>
  <priority_instructions>
    Every byte a tool returns enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. The context-mode tools let you do the work in a sandbox and surface only the derived answer — the raw bytes stay out. Think-in-Code: program the analysis, do not compute it by reading raw data into your conversation.
  </priority_instructions>

  <deferred_tool_bootstrap>
    The context-mode tools below may be DEFERRED in your harness — their schemas are not loaded yet, so calling them directly fails (e.g. "tool not found" / InputValidationError). Load them ONCE before your first ctx_* call:
    ToolSearch(query: "select:mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute,mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search,mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute,mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file,mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index")
    After that they are callable. If any ctx_* call fails as not-found, ToolSearch it and retry — do NOT fall back to Bash/Read just because the schema was not loaded yet.
  </deferred_tool_bootstrap>

  <tool_selection_hierarchy>
    0. MEMORY: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(sort: "timeline")
       - On resume or compaction, query prior decisions, errors, plans, user prompts before asking the user — auto-captured session memory is searchable.
    1. GATHER: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute(commands, queries)
       - Primary research tool. Runs commands in parallel, auto-indexes each output, and (when queries are passed) returns matching sections in the same round trip — no follow-up search call.
       - Each command: {label: "section header", command: "shell command"}; the label becomes the FTS5 chunk title — descriptive labels improve search.
    2. FOLLOW-UP: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(queries: ["q1", "q2", ...])
       - Multiple related questions about anything already indexed (your captures + session memory). Batch every question in one array; the ranking pipeline runs per-query and the round-trip cost is paid once.
    3. PROCESSING: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute(language, code) | mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file(path, language, code)
       - Derive answers FROM data: filter, count, aggregate, parse, transform. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation; the raw bytes stay in the sandbox.
  </tool_selection_hierarchy>

  <when_not_to_use>
    - You intend to PROCESS the output (filter, count, parse, aggregate) → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute or mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute. Bash stays correct when you intend to OBSERVE a short fixed output (git status on a clean tree, whoami, pwd) or when you are mutating state (git, mkdir, rm, mv, navigation).
    - You want to analyze, summarize, or extract from a file → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file. Read stays correct when you intend to Edit the file (Edit needs the exact bytes in your conversation to match against).
    - WebFetch → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index; full network access, results indexed for mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search, raw page bytes never enter your conversation.
    - mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute and mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file for file writes → these run code in a subprocess and discard the sandbox FS; they are for analysis, processing, and computation only.
  </when_not_to_use>

  <file_writing_policy>
    File writes use the native Write or Edit tool — mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute, mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file, and Bash subprocesses do not persist edits to the host filesystem.
    Applies to all file types: code, configs, plans, specs, YAML, JSON, markdown.
  </file_writing_policy>

  <output_constraints>
    <artifact_policy>
      Write artifacts (code, configs, PRDs) to files. Return only: file path + 1-line description.
    </artifact_policy>
  </output_constraints>
  <session_continuity>
    Skills, roles, and decisions captured earlier in this session are a memory aid, not a standing order. Treat them as context that may help — the user's most recent message always takes precedence. If a captured directive conflicts with what the user now asks, follow the user; a past phrase does not bind you.
  </session_continuity>

</context_window_protection>

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
definition.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
definition.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

Use when users need to explain technical concepts, structure presentations or writing, create clear documentation, improve communication clarity, or translate jargon into accessible language. Triggers include requests like "help me explain this clearly", "how do I structure this presentation", "make this less technical", "help me articulate this idea", or any request to simplify complex communication. Do not use for building a slide deck (use five-slides-generator or research-in-5) or for light copyediting of text that is already clear.

# Advisor Tool

You have access to an `advisor` tool backed by a stronger reviewer model. It takes NO parameters -- when you call advisor(), your entire conversation history is automatically forwarded. They see the task, every tool call you've made, every result you've seen.

Call advisor BEFORE substantive work -- before writing, before committing to an interpretation, before building on an assumption. If the task requires orientation first (finding files, fetching a source, seeing what's there), do that, then call advisor. Orientation is not substantive work. Writing, editing, and declaring an answer are.

Also call advisor:
- When you believe the task is complete. BEFORE this call, make your deliverable durable: write the file, save the result, commit the change. The advisor call takes time; if the session ends during it, a durable result persists and an unwritten one doesn't.
- When stuck -- errors recurring, approach not converging, results that don't fit.
- When considering a change of approach.

On tasks longer than a few steps, call advisor at least once before committing to an approach and once before declaring done. On short reactive tasks where the next action is dictated by tool output you just read, you don't need to keep calling -- the advisor adds most of its value on the first call, before the approach crystallizes.

Give the advice serious weight. If you follow a step and it fails empirically, or you have primary-source evidence that contradicts a specific claim (the file says X, the paper states Y), adapt. A passing self-test is not evidence the advice is wrong -- it's evidence your test doesn't check what the advice is checking.

If you've already retrieved data pointing one way and the advisor points another: don't silently switch. Surface the conflict in one more advisor call -- "I found X, you suggest Y, which constraint breaks the tie?" The advisor saw your evidence but may have underweighted it; a reconcile call is cheaper than committing to the wrong branch.
</system-reminder>

Built 2026-09-14 from that day's interview. Eric's diagnosis in his words: projects started on random ideas or suggestions, no deadlines, no staged deliverables, "done is never really defined", and work nobody asked for so nobody to deliver it to. Four earlier fixes (5/22 note, 6/2 morning brief, 6/12 okr-tracker, 7/31 note) died because each needed remembering.

Cap in `meta.slate.cap` (default 4; **5 for Fall 2026 only**). Ideas wait in `/project` ideas. Side lane is outside the cap by Eric's choice.

**Timer:** `KeystoneOS/scripts/ritual-check.ps1` runs `portfolio.py slate-check --json` as the `slate` ritual. Over cap, late step, past finish, missed checkpoint → OVERDUE; incomplete charter or open slot with next_up → DUE. A check that cannot run reports DUE, never OK.

19

21	  dependency means a venv to maintain forever. A read-only local page never
22	  earns that.
23	- **Rendered fresh per request.** Never cached, never regenerated on a timer. A
24	  page that can be stale is a page you stop believing — that is exactly why the
25	  on-demand `project-triage/dashboard.html` never became a front door.

28	  13, because the done-list holds entries no longer in the corpus. It now does
29	  the same **set difference**, and the corpus selection is kept identical across
30	  `server.py`, `gf_gemini.py` and `gf_remaining.py`.
31	- **Judge a running service on its PID, not its last exit code.** A `KeepAlive`
32	  daemon carries the exit code of the instance that *died*, so a restart leaves a
33	  nonzero code behind permanently. `launchctl list`'s first column is the PID and
34	  the second is that stale status — reading the wrong column makes a healthy
35	  service look broken.
36	- **Live `launchctl` state is the truth**; `run-ledger.json` is shown but never
37	  allowed to claim a job succeeded. See [[keystoneos-verification-habits]].
38	- **Every source is optional** — a missing input renders "unknown", never a 500.
39	- **Bound to `127.0.0.1` only**, which is why it needs no auth. Do not change the
40	  bind address without adding one. Read-only on purpose: no buttons, so a stray
41	  browser tab cannot fire an agent. `~/.claude/scripts/skill-button.sh` exists
42	  for the day buttons are wanted.
43	
44	**The threat to a localhost service is a web page you visit, not the network.**
45	Any site your browser opens can make requests to `127.0.0.1`, so binding to
46	loopback is not a security boundary on its own. **DNS rebinding** is the real
47	attack: the attacker's domain re-resolves to `127.0.0.1`, their JavaScript
48	becomes same-origin, and it reads everything. The defence is a **`Host` header
49	allowlist** — refuse any request whose Host is not a loopback name. Three review
50	rounds were needed to get the parsing right: compare IPv6 numerically (so
51	`[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]` is recognised), refuse a second `Host` header rather than
52	guess, strip exactly one trailing DNS dot, and validate the port range. Also
53	learned: **curl silently collapses duplicate headers** — prove that guard over a
54	raw socket.
55	
56	**An allowlisted name is not an allowlisted file.** `Path.exists()` and
57	`read_bytes()` follow symlinks, so an exact-path allowlist still served
58	`/etc/hosts` when the target was swapped for a symlink. Confine the resolved
59	object too, then **read through the same descriptor you checked** (`O_NOFOLLOW`,
60	then compare the fd's `(st_dev, st_ino)` to the pre-check `lstat`) — checking a
61	path and reopening it by name is a check/use race. Close the fd in a `finally`
62	that catches every exception type, not just `OSError`.

65	that contradicts the CLI destroys trust in both. Three separate counters here
66	had to be aligned four times: set difference not arithmetic, the same corpus
67	selection, the same skip gates, the same `GF_MAXBYTES` env override — including
68	its "0 means no cap" convention — and the gate applied to a progress line's
69	numerator *and* denominator.

72	is default-deny, so `daily-backup` exits 1 until the folder is added to
73	`~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`. Working as designed; just add the entry
74	in the same turn. The `class` field answers *who keeps this when you leave
75	Baylor* — `institutional` also copies to Baylor OneDrive ("lost when Baylor
76	access ends"), `personal` stays yours. See [[backup-sync-system]].

90	- **Never add a CORS header to `/api/state.json`, and never open `/os` as
91	  `file://`.** Same-origin is the only thing keeping the whole state object away
92	  from any site the browser has open. A `file://` page would need CORS to fetch it
93	  — that is the trap, not the fix.

- Reading and analyzing file contents

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: EnterWorktree
tools.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

schema.name: Glob
schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). ## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

176	
177	Caught the hang in progress and narrowed it. **Root cause still open** — this section is
178	evidence, not a verdict. Everything below is measured, not inferred:
179	
180	- **It is a hang, not a slow transfer.** Four rsync processes (client `-a ... codex/sessions/`,
181	  its `--server` receiver, plus two older receivers) sat at **0.01–0.03 s of CPU across
182	  34–85 minutes** of wall clock. Zero progress, not slow progress.
183	- **Nothing is left to copy.** The mirror is **256/256 files** — the previously-missing
184	  `2026/08/06/rollout-*.jsonl` is present. A complete mirror still hangs.
185	- **The mount is healthy.** A recursive `find` over the destination returned 256 files
186	  promptly, and `touch` inside the exact hung directory succeeded instantly. Reads *and*
187	  writes both work, so this is not a wedged DriveFS/FUSE mount.
188	- **The wedged processes ignore SIGTERM** (still alive minutes later in `S` state) — they
189	  are blocked inside a call that neither returns nor delivers signals.

193	### Orphans are a symptom, not the cause
194	
195	Two `rsync --server` receivers were **orphaned to PPID 1** (started 13:55 and 14:33). It is
196	tempting to call them the blocker; the timeline refutes it — the **10:31:54 run hung at the
197	identical point** (last line `SNAP skip (missing): .codex/memories`, no end line) while the
198	oldest surviving orphan did not exist until 13:55. `kill` on both orphans did not unblock
199	the live pair either.
200	
201	Why they accumulate: **`daily-backup.ps1` contains no `pkill` at all** (verified by grep —
202	do not go looking for one). The anchored `pkill -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` belongs to an *ad-hoc
203	wrapper used interactively in another session*. That pattern matches only the client, whose
204	`argv[0]` is the full path; the `--server` child's `argv[0]` is bare `rsync`, so
205	`pgrep -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` returns the client alone. Every kill-and-retry therefore strands
206	one more receiver. If that wrapper is reused, match on `-x rsync` or the destination path.

208	### ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-14 17:00 — it is not rsync
209	
210	Ran the copy in the foreground with `-avv`, unpiped. It printed ~99 lines of
211	`... is uptodate` and froze mid-filename. Then:
212	
213	- `sample <receiver-pid>` showed the process blocked in **`__mmap`** — one frame, not moving.
214	- `lsof` on it showed FD 5 open on a specific **destination** file:
215	  `codex/sessions/2026/05/08/rollout-2026-05-08T17-14-58-019e09a8-*.jsonl`.
216	- **`head -c 512` on that destination file hangs by itself**, with zero rsync processes
217	  running. A plain read. So the file is unreadable through DriveFS.
218	- A 44-file sample elsewhere in the same mirror read instantly, so it is **specific files,
219	  not the mount**.
220	
221	The files are **DriveFS placeholders** — uploaded to Google, then evicted from the local
222	cache. Census of the destination on 2026-08-14: 256 files, **122 materialized (48.5 MB on
223	disk), 134 placeholder-only (240.7 MB logical, 0 bytes local)**. Source is 256/256
224	materialized. Detect with `stat -f '%b %z'`: blocks==0 with a nonzero logical size means
225	the content is not local. Reading one forces an on-demand fetch, and that fetch stalls —
226	which is what blocks `__mmap`. rsync was the victim, not the cause. **Do not chase rsync
227	flags**; the block happens at open, before any comparison strategy applies.
228	
229	**This inverts the problem: the backup is fine, the verification is what's broken.** All
230	256 files are on Google's servers. Nothing is missing. What fails is the *next* run's
231	attempt to re-read them to confirm they match. Never conclude "the snapshot is broken"
232	from this failure mode.
233	
234	Also: `du -sh` on the destination reports the *local cache* (48 MB), not the logical 289 MB.
235	Both numbers are true and mean different things — do not treat the gap as missing data.
236	
237	Diagnostic sequence that worked, reuse it: `sample <pid>` for the blocking syscall →
238	`lsof -p <pid>` for the file it is on → bounded `head -c` on that path to prove the
239	filesystem, not the tool, is at fault.

**Current state (2026-09-03).** Two backup runs happen on most days, and the 09-02 entry was
right about that — but **not** because reconcile hard-codes the backup. The real mechanism,
traced 09-03:

`keystone-reconcile.ps1` is a **generic make-up engine**. It has no mention of `daily-backup` at
all; it loops the registry at `DEV/KeystoneOS/data/jobs.json` and calls
`run-job.ps1 -Job <id> -Trigger reconcile -MadeUp` for any job with no success recorded today.
The `daily-backup` job is in that registry with `reconcile: true`, `graceMinutes: 60`,
`maxAttemptsPerDay: 2`, and `makeupWindow: 07:00-20:00`. Its `successProbe` greps today's
`daily-backup.log` for `daily-backup end: OK`. So:

- **If no successful run is recorded by 07:00, reconcile replays it** → the ~07:00-07:10 run.
- **launchd `com.keystone.dailybackup` fires at 09:00 regardless** → the second run.
- **Run the backup by hand before 07:00 and reconcile skips it** ("already succeeded today").
  Confirmed 09-03: a 06:15 manual run logged `OK` at 06:25, and no 07:00 run happened.

Registry inconsistency worth knowing: `jobs.json` records `schedule.at: "00:30"` while the live
plist fires at 09:00. The make-up window is what actually drives the 07:00 replay, so the stale
`at` has not bitten yet. Still true: `launchctl ... runs = 0` proves nothing — read the log.
Receipts cluster only on days CRASHBOX is attached: a mount gap, not a schedule gap.

**"Scheduled runs cannot push" is NOT yet established — and the two contexts differ.** On
2026-09-03 the **09:00 launchd** run pushed `global-memory` cleanly and ended `OK (0 errors)`:
no `PUSH FAILED`, no `PUSH ERR`. But the **reconcile/`run-job.ps1`** context — which is where the
09-02 07:08 and 08-13 07:00 failures happened — **was not exercised that day**, because the manual
06:15 run pre-empted the replay. Do not read 09-03 as clearing the gap; it only clears launchd.
`daily-backup.ps1:74` no longer swallows the reason: the `Out-Null` was replaced 09-03 with
captured output that logs `REPO <name> : PUSH ERR | <text>` on failure only. **The error text will
only appear on a day nobody runs the backup by hand before 07:00.** Diagnose from that line rather
than assuming a credential gap. `daily-backup.err` is stale (last written 2026-08-06); never read
it as current. Manual remedy after a failed push is still `git -C <repo> push origin main` for
SecondBrain, `.claude/global-memory`, `.claude`.

**SSD layout:** non-repo DEV dirs land in `DEV-nonrepo/`, **not** `DEV/` — there is no `DEV/`
on CRASHBOX (roots are `DEV-nonrepo/`, `DEV-repo-data/`, `DEV-working-tree/`, `claude/`,
`codex/`, `gemini/`, `SecondBrain/`, `_receipts/`). `._`-prefixed files beside every real file
are normal AppleDouble xattr sidecars on exFAT, not corruption or duplication.

The nightly backup is `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` (pwsh, launchd
`com.keystone.dailybackup`), driven by `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`, logging to
`~/.claude/scripts/logs/daily-backup.log`. `~/.claude` is itself the `dotclaude` repo.
Workflow docs live in `~/DEV/Bucket` (`docs/SYSTEM-HEALTH-FINDINGS.md`,
`docs/AGENT-FIX-PROMPT.md`, `docs/FIX-STATUS-2026-08-14.md`).

## The root cause behind most "divergence" symptoms — CLOSED 2026-08-14

The retired **Windows box was still running `daily-backup.ps1` and pushing to the shared
repos** (SecondBrain, dotclaude, claude-skills, claude-global-memory). Two writers on one
set of repos manufactured `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` nightly. Identified by the
commit-message format `chore: daily backup sync YYYY-MM-DD [auto]`, generated at
`daily-backup.ps1:62`.

**Retired 2026-08-14**: all 9 KeystoneOS/MorningBriefing scheduled tasks disabled (not
unregistered) on the Windows box; all four repos left at 0 ahead / 0 behind. It contributed
no unique history since 08-05 — only two append-only Windows failure logs, preserved
byte-identical to `~/Desktop/windows-retirement-2026-08-14/` on that machine and
deliberately **not** pushed (origin had already untracked `.memsearch-index.log` in
`a0e58c9`; committing would have undone a Mac-side decision).

**Update 2026-09-10: the Windows laptop is ACTIVE again** (synced 9/9; both machines in use).
The retirement above is history, not current state. Unverified: whether its disabled
scheduled tasks were re-enabled. Before blaming a single writer for `repo-diverged`, check
the Windows task list and look for `[auto]` commits from it.

Residual, by design — the box is meant to stay usable:
- **Session hooks still write.** `settings.json` `Stop`/`SessionEnd` hooks write
  `global-memory/transcripts/`, so interactive Claude Code use there re-dirties that repo.
  It cannot *diverge* it — nothing pushes on a schedule anymore. (That Stop hook is
  currently broken there anyway: `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on a mangled
  `C:\Program Files\Git\...\transcript-capture.js` path.)
- **`daily-backup.ps1` on Windows is still the macOS port** and still buggy. It is inert

- Three non-KeystoneOS tasks left enabled (`CFB-ForecastCaptureReminder`,

## Manifest classification — get this right, it routes athlete data

`backup-manifest.json` is default-deny: any `~/DEV` dir absent from `paths[]` fails the
health check. Adding an entry requires a human class call:

| class | destinations |
|---|---|
| `institutional` | `ssd`, `baylor` (+`github` if a repo) |
| `personal` | `ssd` (+`github` if a repo) |

`isRepo: true` also sets `captureOrphans` and `captureWorkingTree` true and needs `remote`.
**Athlete data must never be classed `personal`** — `personal` skips the Baylor OneDrive
destination. `baylor` is `deprecated: true` and must never be a sole destination.

## Traps that cost time

- **Milvus is NOT in the memsearch path**, despite what `RESTORE.md` and the Bucket docs
  say. Indexing works with port 19530 closed and Docker not installed. Don't set it up.
- **`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path.** It passes `rsync -n`, which writes nothing. A
  snapshot that fails live will show `OK` in a dry run. Only a non-dry run is evidence.
- **Never size up a DriveFS destination with `du`.** It reports local cache/allocated
  blocks, not logical size — the `codex/sessions` mirror read as "47 MB of 289 MB" while
  actually holding 255 of 256 files, with a 35 MB file verified byte-identical by
  `stat -f%z` on both sides. Compare **file counts and per-file byte sizes**, never `du -sh`.
- **`snapshot:sessions` is a genuine hang** — not a size problem, not a lock, not a
  permission fault, and not slow enumeration. Three wrong theories died here in one
  session; see the evidence section below before forming a fourth. **Bounded 2026-08-14**
  by a watchdog in `Invoke-Rsync` (900s ceiling, hard SIGKILL, records `rsync-timeout`),
  committed as `8863a37`. That caps the symptom so the run reaches the SSD capture. The
  wedge itself is still unexplained.
- **Tier A memory is NOT in git.** `~/.claude/.gitignore` line 1 is `/*` (default-deny
  allowlist) and `projects/` is not allowlisted, so `projects/*/memory/*.md` has exactly
  two backup layers: the Drive SNAP of `~/.claude/projects`, and the SSD. With CRASHBOX
  unmounted that is a single copy. Nothing to "commit" there — it's by design.
- **`daily-backup.ps1` refuses to merge diverged repos by design** — that's correct
  behavior, not a bug. Reconcile by hand.
- **stack-doctor's cloud heartbeat** watches the newest per-run receipt
  (`_receipts/run-*.txt`). It used to watch `RESTORE.md`, which the job *copies*
  (`Copy-Item -Force`, line 411) rather than rewrites, so its mtime never advanced and the
  check cried `backup-cloud-stale (218h)` while DriveFS was healthy. Fixed 2026-08-14.
- **Untracked files block a fast-forward**, and plain `git stash` does not pick them up —
  needs `-u`, or rename them aside. Bit the documented SecondBrain fix.
- Reading exit codes through a pipe returns the *last* pipeline element's status, not the
  command's — see [[zsh-shell-traps]]. This produced two wrong readings in one
  session (`rsync ... | tail` and a stack-check run).

## Standing state as of 2026-08-14

Fixed: `Invoke-Rsync` false-OK guard, 6 manifest entries, SecondBrain reconciled (both
machines' briefings preserved, Mac copies renamed `*.mac-local.md`), stack-doctor cloud
heartbeat. Morning brief **retired** at Eric's request — `com.keystone.morningbriefing`
booted out + disabled, plist and `~/DEV/morning-briefing` retained, dropped from
stack-doctor's checked sets. `com.keystone.morning` is a *different* KeystoneOS cadence —
leave it alone.

CRASHBOX SSD **reattached 2026-08-14 ~11:50** (`/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup`, 447 GB
free, writable) — first orphan/working-tree capture since migration due in the next
nightly. Bucket doc set committed + pushed (`ce94371`). Windows retired (above).

Two script fixes committed 2026-08-14 beyond the ones above: `ac2af1d` guards the script
against running on a non-macOS host (it is the macOS port; `$IsMacOS` is PS6+, so
Windows PowerShell 5.1's undefined `$null` aborts too — intended), and `8863a37` adds the
`Invoke-Rsync` watchdog. Both are in dotclaude, so any machine pulling the repo inherits
them.

Open: the `codex/sessions` wedge itself (bounded, not explained — see evidence below).
`.errors.log` retains 6 historical lines — clear the file once one clean nightly lands
with the Windows box off, not before.

**Acceptance test — run 2026-08-14 15:48, mostly PASSED.** `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` and
`manifest-unmanaged` are both GONE (Windows retirement + manifest work confirmed). The
watchdog fired at 900s exactly as designed, killed the wedge, and the run *continued* —
so the **SSD layer captured for the first time since 2026-08-06**: 53,533 files newer than
the old receipt, `RECEIPT ssd : verified run=20260814-154848`, ~24 GB total including
Risk_Stratification_Engine 2.0 GB and ForcePlate_DecisionSystem 1.6 GB.

Remaining: `ERROR (2 errors)` = `rsync-timeout` + `snapshot:sessions`, which are the same
single `codex/sessions` wedge counted twice (the watchdog error plus the snapshot failure
it causes). Not two problems. Clear `.errors.log` only after the wedge itself is fixed.

Verification trap met here: `find -newermt '-30 minutes'` silently matches nothing on BSD
find (macOS) — it wants an absolute date. Use `find -newer <reference-file>` instead. Also
remember `rsync -a` preserves source mtimes, so freshly-copied files look old; compare
*directory* mtimes or use a reference file to prove a capture ran.

Note the run ordering: Drive SNAPs run *before* the SSD capture, so a long `codex/sessions`
seed delays the SSD layer within a given run. Not a failure, just a wait.

## `snapshot:sessions` — evidence from a live reproduction, 2026-08-14 15:20 (stack-doctor)

Caught the hang in progress and narrowed it. **Root cause still open** — this section is
evidence, not a verdict. Everything below is measured, not inferred:

- **It is a hang, not a slow transfer.** Four rsync processes (client `-a ... codex/sessions/`,
  its `--server` receiver, plus two older receivers) sat at **0.01–0.03 s of CPU across
  34–85 minutes** of wall clock. Zero progress, not slow progress.
- **Nothing is left to copy.** The mirror is **256/256 files** — the previously-missing
  `2026/08/06/rollout-*.jsonl` is present. A complete mirror still hangs.
- **The mount is healthy.** A recursive `find` over the destination returned 256 files
  promptly, and `touch` inside the exact hung directory succeeded instantly. Reads *and*
  writes both work, so this is not a wedged DriveFS/FUSE mount.
- **The wedged processes ignore SIGTERM** (still alive minutes later in `S` state) — they
  are blocked inside a call that neither returns nor delivers signals.
- **Dry runs cannot see it**: `-n` completes clean, live runs hang. Another instance of the
  "`-DryRun` cannot verify a write path" trap above.

### Orphans are a symptom, not the cause

Two `rsync --server` receivers were **orphaned to PPID 1** (started 13:55 and 14:33). It is
tempting to call them the blocker; the timeline refutes it — the **10:31:54 run hung at the
identical point** (last line `SNAP skip (missing): .codex/memories`, no end line) while the
oldest surviving orphan did not exist until 13:55. `kill` on both orphans did not unblock
the live pair either.

Why they accumulate: **`daily-backup.ps1` contains no `pkill` at all** (verified by grep —
do not go looking for one). The anchored `pkill -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` belongs to an *ad-hoc
wrapper used interactively in another session*. That pattern matches only the client, whose
`argv[0]` is the full path; the `--server` child's `argv[0]` is bare `rsync`, so
`pgrep -f "^/usr/bin/rsync"` returns the client alone. Every kill-and-retry therefore strands
one more receiver. If that wrapper is reused, match on `-x rsync` or the destination path.

### ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-14 17:00 — it is not rsync

Ran the copy in the foreground with `-avv`, unpiped. It printed ~99 lines of
`... is uptodate` and froze mid-filename. Then:

- `sample <receiver-pid>` showed the process blocked in **`__mmap`** — one frame, not moving.
- `lsof` on it showed FD 5 open on a specific **destination** file:
  `codex/sessions/2026/05/08/rollout-2026-05-08T17-14-58-019e09a8-*.jsonl`.
- **`head -c 512` on that destination file hangs by itself**, with zero rsync processes
  running. A plain read. So the file is unreadable through DriveFS.
- A 44-file sample elsewhere in the same mirror read instantly, so it is **specific files,
  not the mount**.

The files are **DriveFS placeholders** — uploaded to Google, then evicted from the local
cache. Census of the destination on 2026-08-14: 256 files, **122 materialized (48.5 MB on
disk), 134 placeholder-only (240.7 MB logical, 0 bytes local)**. Source is 256/256
materialized. Detect with `stat -f '%b %z'`: blocks==0 with a nonzero logical size means
the content is not local. Reading one forces an on-demand fetch, and that fetch stalls —
which is what blocks `__mmap`. rsync was the victim, not the cause. **Do not chase rsync
flags**; the block happens at open, before any comparison strategy applies.

**This inverts the problem: the backup is fine, the verification is what's broken.** All
256 files are on Google's servers. Nothing is missing. What fails is the *next* run's
attempt to re-read them to confirm they match. Never conclude "the snapshot is broken"
from this failure mode.

Also: `du -sh` on the destination reports the *local cache* (48 MB), not the logical 289 MB.
Both numbers are true and mean different things — do not treat the gap as missing data.

Diagnostic sequence that worked, reuse it: `sample <pid>` for the blocking syscall →
`lsof -p <pid>` for the file it is on → bounded `head -c` on that path to prove the
filesystem, not the tool, is at fault.

**Attempted fix that DID NOT WORK**: pinning `My Drive/Backups` "Available offline" via the
Finder context menu (there is no CLI or xattr for it — the app ships no control surface).
Eric pinned it 2026-08-14 17:30. Result: **one** file materialized, then flat for 5 minutes
(133 placeholders, 49.2 MB, unchanged). Restarting Drive did not help either.

**DriveFS on this Mac is itself unhealthy** — this is the real blocker, not rsync and not
the pin:
- It refused a graceful `osascript quit` for 20s and needed SIGKILL. Its log emitted
  `crashpad ... ThreadsStuck` every 6s. Restarting cleared the stuck threads but nothing else.
- The **download** queue fails, not just uploads: `merger.cc:969:ProcessDownloadEvent` +
  `HandleFailedChange [DownloadMergeQueueItem]`. DriveFS cannot pull content *down*.
- Signs of local DB damage: `item_query_handler.cc:1135:OnGetItemIds Ignoring item
  local-376561 that's missing from ...`.
- NOT quota: 671 GB used of 5.5 TB.

**Do not clear the DriveFS content cache as the remedy.** It converts every materialized
file into a placeholder needing re-download, feeding the exact mechanism that is failing —
122 readable files could become 0. If DriveFS is repaired, do it by signing out and back in
to force a DB rebuild, deliberately, with time to watch it.

### RESOLVED 2026-08-14 — the backup was never broken, the verification was

**Final mechanism**: files Drive has evicted from local cache are placeholders. Fetching a
placeholder through DriveFS is *unreliable* — usually fast, sometimes stalling for tens of
minutes. rsync blocking on such a fetch is the entire "wedge". Proof it is a slow fetch and
not a poisoned file: the file that hung four separate times **now reads instantly**, and its
blocks went 0 → 770,048 — the repeated read attempts eventually completed the fetch. Six
other placeholders read fine first try. Nothing was corrupt.

**`~/.claude/scripts/verify-drive-backup.sh` (`0d2edb5`) is now the way to verify.** It
compares the Drive API's server-side `md5Checksum` against a local md5 — metadata only, no
DriveFS read, batched ~25 names per query. First run on `~/.codex/sessions`:
**256/256 verified, 0 mismatch, 0 missing.** The snapshot that logged `FAILED` for days was
complete and byte-correct the whole time.

Do not "fix" this by deleting Drive copies. Both files that hung were verified byte-identical
to source *before* anything was touched — deleting would have destroyed a good backup to
repair a read path.

**It is plain fetch latency, scaling with file size** — no mystery left. A full read-scan of
all 256 files with a 6s per-file cap: 33 stalled, and those averaged **2,301 KB vs 1,156 KB
for the set overall** (max 15.8 MB). Bigger file, longer fetch. Nothing file-specific,
nothing corrupt. The scan itself moved the mirror from 122 → 230 materialized (48.5 → 161.8 MB
local), which is exactly what "reading materializes it" predicts.

Caution when testing this: **reading a file materializes it**, so any scan warms the cache and
a later run passes for reasons that will not hold once Drive evicts again. Timestamp results
and never treat a post-scan rsync run as a clean verification.

### Why DriveFS is unhealthy — found 2026-08-14 18:20

**Google Drive is mirroring `~/DEV` as a device-backup folder named "My Mac"**, including
**34 `.git` directories / 3,470 files**. VS Code has `"git.autofetch": true`, which rewrites
every repo's `FETCH_HEAD` on a 180s cycle; Drive uploads all 34 each time. That is the source
of the `PRECONDITION_FAILED` storms on `FETCH_HEAD` and the stuck threads in `drive_fs.txt`,
and therefore of the slow placeholder fetches upstream.

Proof (not inference): local `~/DEV/*/.git/FETCH_HEAD` all stamped 18:22:09 while Drive's
server copies read `2026-08-14T23:22:09Z` — same second — and the Drive parent chain resolves
`FETCH_HEAD → .git → DataBase_GPS_Reporting → DEV → My Mac`.

**`OneDrive-Import` was a red herring** — it holds 22 `.git` dirs / 7,292 files, but they are
static archives and do not churn. Don't chase it.

**FIXED 2026-08-14 ~18:28 — Eric removed `~/DEV` from Drive Preferences → "Folders from your
computer" (keeping the cloud copy). Verified, and it worked:**
- Server-side `FETCH_HEAD` froze at `23:28:12Z` while local `~/DEV` copies kept updating
  (18:32:28) — churn decoupled, `git.autofetch` left ON as intended.
- `PRECONDITION_FAILED` 14 → **0**. `ProcessDownloadEvent` errors 11 → **0**.
  `HandleFailedChange` stable (idle retry backlog, not growing).
- Google Drive CPU **64.6% → 0.0%**.
- **End-to-end: 5/5 genuine placeholders (blocks==0) fetched in 2–3s each**, where the same
  class of read previously stalled for minutes or indefinitely. This is the actual cure for
  the `snapshot:sessions` wedge — the watchdog only bounded it.

Original recommendation, for the record: remove `~/DEV` from Drive Preferences → "Folders
from your computer", choosing KEEP for the existing cloud copy. The mirror is redundant and
strictly worse than the nightly, which already covers `~/DEV` via 68 manifest entries →
SSD + GitHub with `.git` excluded and credential files denied (6 projects hit that policy on
2026-08-14). **Do not** "fix" this by disabling `git.autofetch`: that masks the symptom, costs
a useful feature, and leaves 3,470 `.git` files still mirrored to churn on every commit and
checkout. Verify afterward by re-querying `FETCH_HEAD` modifiedTime via the Drive API and
re-checking `drive_fs.txt` for `ThreadsStuck` / `PRECONDITION_FAILED`.

How to check whether anything is pending before any Drive surgery: sample
`grep -c HandleModifiedLocalItem/HandleFailedChange/DownloadMergeQueueItem` in
`~/Library/Application Support/Google/DriveFS/Logs/drive_fs.txt` over ~90s — flat counters
mean idle queues. **Do not** use the presence of `com.google.drivefs.item-id` as an
upload-pending signal: 774 files in Backups lacked it and were all already on the server.

Rejected: `--ignore-existing` (would freeze any mid-session rollout file at its partial
size in Drive permanently) and leaving the watchdog to absorb it (~15 min wasted nightly,
and two standing errors would camouflage real ones).

Note `-W` (whole-file) is already default for local transfers, so `--whole-file`,
`--size-only` and delta-algorithm tuning are all dead ends here — the block happens on
open, before any comparison strategy matters.

## The SSD layer's real failure mode — schedule/mount mismatch, found 2026-08-29

**The nightly is healthy; the SSD layer is simply absent at run time.** `com.keystone.dailybackup`
fires at 00:30 and CRASHBOX is normally unplugged then, so every run logs
`TARGET SSD /Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup NOT MOUNTED - orphan and working-tree capture
SKIPPED this run` and ends `OK (0 errors)`. A clean exit code is therefore **not** evidence the
SSD captured — the skip is not an error. Check `_receipts/run-*.txt` mtime on the drive instead.

Receipt history proves the pattern: 10 SSD captures total, clustered on days the drive happened
to be attached (Aug 6, Aug 14 ×5, Aug 15, Aug 16, Aug 17), then a **12-day gap** to Aug 29. Eric
read this as "the SSD backup has never run"; it had, just rarely.

**Manual run is the remedy and takes ~6 minutes**, not the ~45 the 2026-08-14 notes imply:
`/opt/homebrew/bin/pwsh -File ~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` (no SSD-only switch exists; do
not add one). Run 20260829-073713: Drive SNAPs finished in **6 seconds** — the `codex/sessions`
wedge is genuinely gone since the `~/DEV` de-mirroring fix — DEV capture 07:37–07:40, `.claude`/
`.codex`/`.gemini`/SecondBrain state 07:41–07:42, `RECEIPT ssd : verified` at 07:42:50,
`end: OK (0 errors)` at 07:43:14. SSD 25 → 27 GB. The long tail in the 00:34 nightly was the
memsearch INDEX step (00:51→01:18), which runs *after* the backup and is not part of it.

Verification trap repeated here: **top-level SSD directory mtimes stay old after a successful
capture** (`SecondBrain` still read Aug 17, `claude` Aug 14) because `rsync -a` preserves source
mtimes and a parent dir's mtime only moves when an entry is added or removed at that level. The
`STATE-SSD ... : OK` log lines and the receipt are the evidence; mtimes are not. See also
[[keystoneos-verification-habits]].

**RESOLVED 2026-08-29**: schedule moved 00:30 -> 09:00 in
`~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.keystone.dailybackup.plist` (PlistBuddy `Set :StartCalendarInterval:Hour 9`,
then `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.dailybackup` + `bootstrap`; live schedule confirmed
`Hour => 9, Minute => 0` via `launchctl print`). Old plist kept at `.plist.bak-2026-08-29`. 09:00 was
chosen from mount evidence (drive attached 07:31 on 08-29; the 08-17 capture ran 08:05). **Do not
verify this by mtime or by exit code** — the only proof is a fresh `_receipts/run-*.txt` on the drive
dated 08-30 or later. If receipts still cluster, the drive is not attached at 09:00 and the hour is wrong.

`~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` archived to `.errors.log.archived-2026-08-29` and
cleared the same day. It held two **still-open** issues, not stale history: memsearch `onnxruntime`
import failure (2026-08-22, corroborated by `INDEX full set: Indexed 0 chunks` on 08-28/08-29), and
stack-doctor weekly flagging `errors-log`, `flush-stale`, `memfile-full:MEMORY.md` (2026-08-24).

**Both cleared by end of 2026-08-29** — stack-doctor returned `ALL CLEAR`: memsearch `search: OK`,
`last-flush.json OK (0h ago)`, no `FLUSH_ERROR` in recent dailies, `errors.log: clean`. The
`onnxruntime` import failure did not need a reinstall, so **do not** reflexively run
`uv tool install --force memsearch` on the next `ETIMEDOUT` — that strips the local flush patch
and creates a worse problem. Confirmed here: `memsearch --version` answered instantly (0.4.17) and
`pgrep -fc memsearch` was 0, ruling out both a broken binary and the
[[milvus-lock-misdiagnosis]] lock-contention pattern.

A separate `memsearch-sync: index ETIMEDOUT Nx consecutively` streak ran 6→13 during the afternoon
session of 08-29 and then self-cleared. Per the skill's own note, `Indexed 0 chunks` is usually a
starved flush pipeline rather than a dead indexer — **check `flush-stale` before touching
memsearch**. The streak counter is reset by the nightly backup, so a climbing count mid-session is
expected noise unless it survives a backup run. Both cleared by end of 2026-08-29 —
stack-doctor returned ALL CLEAR and the thread is closed.

Guard trap: shell truncation (`: > file`) anywhere under `$HOME` is blocked by dcg
rule `core.filesystem:redirect-truncate-root-home`; `cp /dev/null file` is allowed, and macOS has no
`truncate` binary. This file is itself near the `memfile-full` threshold — trim before appending more.

## A stalled run with no rsync child = an unanswered macOS access prompt (2026-09-03)

`daily-backup.ps1` gates both optional destinations on a bare `Test-Path` with **no timeout**:
`Test-Path $GDrive` (section 2a) and `Test-Path $SsdRoot` (section 2b). When macOS has a pending
TCC/removable-volume permission prompt for that path, the call blocks **forever** — and because 2a
runs before 2b, the SSD capture never happens and no receipt is written.

**The tell:** `pwsh` alive in `S`/`SN` state, **zero rsync children**, and the log frozen mid-run.
That is not a slow copy — a slow copy always shows an `rsync` process. `ps -axo pid,stat,comm` on
macOS marks I/O wait `U`, not `D`; a `D`-state grep finds nothing and proves nothing.

**The fix is the human, not the shell — look at the screen for a pending prompt FIRST.** On
2026-09-03 both `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-*` and `/Volumes/CRASHBOX` were unresponsive to
a plain `ls`. The Drive half cleared after a quit/relaunch of Google Drive, **but Eric was
approving access prompts in that same window — the relaunch is unproven and may have done nothing.**
Do not treat killing Google Drive as the known fix. The SSD half cleared only when he approved the
prompt. **Do not force-unmount CRASHBOX** (exFAT, no journal) — ask first.

Probably (unverified): the Claude Code shell and the launchd/reconcile jobs are different TCC
principals, so this prompt should not recur for the scheduled runs — but it may fire once per new
app that launches the script.

**Never re-run without `pkill -f daily-backup.ps1` first.** A hung run is harmless, but several hung
runs unblock *together* the moment access is granted and race onto the SSD — the two-writer
corruption this whole system exists to prevent.

**Timing that matters:** reconcile replays the backup at 07:00 if no `OK` is logged for today, and
launchd fires at 09:00 regardless (see "Current state" above). A manual run finishing before 07:00
suppresses the replay; one finishing after 07:00 can collide with it.

Open gap, not yet fixed: neither `Test-Path` has a watchdog, unlike `Invoke-Rsync`
(`$RsyncTimeoutSec = 900`). Worth wrapping both.

## `/backup` skill + the completeness signal (2026-09-04)

`~/.claude/skills/backup/SKILL.md` is the on-demand path — the launchd job only fires if the
Mac is awake at 09:00. Standing routine: plug in CRASHBOX, then type `/backup`.

**Job count, not error count, is the completeness signal.** A run with CRASHBOX unmounted
reports `OK (0 errors)` with **9 jobs**; the same run with it attached reports **31 jobs**.
Never report "backup complete" from a 0-error run without checking `okCount` and naming any
skipped target.

`repo-push:*` failures are usually a transient `Could not resolve host: github.com`, not a
credential or repo problem — commits are already local, so a re-run pushes them. Seen
2026-09-04 09:05 on `global-memory` and `skills`; one re-run cleared both.

A USB-C drive that powers on but never mounts is almost always a charge-only cable.
`diskutil list external` printing nothing at all is the fast check — that is a cable/port
problem, not software.

Full handoff: `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-09-04-backup-skill.md`.

## Manifest coverage closed + job-count baseline reset (2026-09-09)

**The 49 `manifest-unmanaged` folders are gone.** They were never a classification backlog —
they were fallout from the GitHub consolidation migration (see [[github-consolidation]]).
All 49 added to `backup-manifest.json` in one pass: 47 are git repos with `erash11` remotes
(`isRepo:true`, `captureOrphans`/`captureWorkingTree` true, destinations `["ssd","github"]`),
and 2 are plain dirs — `_ARCHIVE` (4.3 GB) and `docs` — destinations `["ssd"]` only.
`baylor` deliberately omitted from every new entry; it is deprecated and Eric's own newest
entry (`DEV/Life-OS`, commit `3444c0b`) already omits it.

**`class` is inert.** Grep of `daily-backup.ps1` shows it is read nowhere — only `isRepo`,
`captureOrphans`, `captureWorkingTree` and `destinations` drive behavior. The
institutional/personal call is documentation. Do not stall a manifest add waiting on it.

**A DEV manifest entry never auto-commits or pushes that repo.** `Sync-Repo` is called on a
hardcoded list (SecondBrain, global-memory, skills, dotclaude); the manifest loop only calls
`Capture-RepoData` (SSD) or `Snapshot-Additive`. Adding 47 project repos was therefore safe
with open PRs and dirty trees — verify from source before assuming otherwise.

**Job-count baseline is now 76, not 31.** The 2026-09-04 note above (9 = no SSD, 31 = SSD
attached) is superseded. Full run with CRASHBOX attached = **76 jobs**. `CAPTURE` only logs a
line when a repo has files git does not carry, so 18 log lines with 65 capture jobs is normal —
read `okCount`, not the log line count.

**Removed 2 dead entries**: `DEV/AI_Analyst` and `DEV/token-dashboard`. Both had moved into
`~/DEV/_ARCHIVE/`, which is itself now backed up, so coverage was preserved, not dropped.
`DexaProject` stays declared-but-absent on purpose — it lives on Google Drive.

**`~/.claude` now tracks session transcripts.** Eric's commit `8a3d55c` (2026-09-09 15:44)
un-ignored `projects/`, so the dotclaude repo carries ~368 MB of `.jsonl` transcripts and
Tier A memory. This **invalidates the "Tier A memory is NOT in git" trap above** — it now has
a third layer. No single file exceeds 40 MB, so pushes succeed; they are just slower.

Full handoff: `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-09-09-backup-manifest-coverage.md`.
